entries.title: Singapore is paying people to read books – can it fix the reading crisis?
entries.summary: A government scheme is giving citizens cash for spending time with a good book. We ask behavioural scientists, along with The Anxious Generation author and psychologist Jonathan Haidt, whether it’ll help make the habit stickCould the solution to the reading crisis lie in paying people to put down their phones and pick up a book? That’s what one government, at least, is resorting to: this month, Si
entries.content:
Could the solution to the reading crisis lie in paying people to put down their phones and pick up a book? That’s what one government, at least, is resorting to: this month, Singapore launched a scheme promising actual cash to citizens as a reward for logging reading time on a government website.

It’s unlikely to make you megabucks – you have to rack up 50 reading sessions of at least 15 minutes to earn one Singapore dollar (£0.59), with only one logged session allowed per day. But behavioural scientists and psychologists told the Guardian such a scheme could still help boost a habit in precipitous decline.

Jonathan Haidt, a psychologist and the author of the bestselling book The Anxious Generation, about the impact of social media on young people’s mental health, says that some children are highly motivated by money, and “all kids respond to rewards to some degree” – so for young people, the scheme is “likely to have some beneficial effect in setting up a habit of reading”. Lory Barile, associate professor in economics at the University of Warwick, adds that “there is good evidence that repeating a behaviour consistently can help it become more automatic over time”.

If participants find reading “pleasurable in itself”, then the habit may stick, says Haidt. Yet, for some, the monetary reward “will convey to them that they are reading only for the extrinsic reward”, and so when the money stops, the reading will, too. Barile agrees that the most interesting question isn’t whether people read more while they’re being rewarded, but whether the scheme “helps people establish a reading habit that persists once the reward is no longer present”.

While the earning potential of the Singapore scheme is low, this doesn’t necessarily mean it won’t be effective, says Ivo Vlaev, a professor of behavioural psychology at the National University of Singapore. “One of the interesting findings from behavioural science is that incentives do not always work in proportion to their monetary value.”

The scheme shouldn’t be thought of as “paying people to read” in a conventional economic sense – a dollar every few weeks is obviously not enough to compensate participants for the time they’ve invested. Instead, the payment “may be acting more as a trigger than as a wage”, says Vlaev. Logging reading time and accumulating points means participants “receive an immediate signal that the behaviour has been recognised, your streak continues and you make progress towards a goal”. And once someone has actually started reading, “the intrinsic rewards of the activity can take over”, he adds.

We all know reading has long-term benefits, but a key element of the Singapore scheme hinges on introducing a short-term reward for the activity, mimicking the immediate dopamine hit of scrolling. In fact, the “gamified” element may be “smarter” than the financial reward offered, says Patrick Taylor, director of education at the Behavioural Insights Team (which originated in David Cameron’s Cabinet Office, also known as the “nudge unit”). “Having a manageable 15-minute daily goal, built around existing routines like commuting or bedtime, with streaks and tracking to keep progress visible” are the aspects that could make the scheme a success, he says.

Such a scheme may be particularly effective for lapsed readers. “If people are already intrinsically motivated to read, this may be enough to tip them over the edge to read a bit more,” says Katy Milkman, a professor at Wharton business school, University of Pennsylvania. Vlaev adds that “if somebody already intends to read but repeatedly fails to get started, a tiny immediate reward can help bridge the gap between intention and action”.

In the UK, non-monetary reward schemes for reading and other types of learning have long been in place, such as the primary school rainbow certificate scheme, through which “the value comes primarily from recognition and a sense of achievement”, says Barile. The Reading Agency’s Summer Reading Challenge allows children to receive badges and certificates for reading, too.

A UK pilot of the Singapore-style scheme could therefore “compare small financial rewards with symbolic rewards such as certificates or badges, as well as gamification, goal-setting and progress feedback”, says Barile. Others agree that such schemes should be run as trials, “so we find out what works and why”, says Taylor. Haidt suggests a few variations to test: some children could be randomly assigned to be paid in cash, others could be paid in free books of their choice (“so that they see books as a reward, not money as a reward for reading”), and others “are simply urged to read to get points in a competition, no money”. A fourth group “would be a true control, nothing is done, other than measuring how many books they read”.

But the question remains: should governments financially reward what has been traditionally considered something you do for fun? Milkman sees it differently: “We subsidise, and even require, many other forms of education.” So why not reward reading, too?

entries.title: No Land to Stand On by Mahmoud Khalil review – a searing account of political imprisonment
entries.summary: The Palestinian Columbia student snatched by ICE writes about his Kafkaesque ordeal with a quiet furyMahmoud Khalil was completing a master’s degree at Columbia University when, in March 2025, plain-clothed officers from the Department of Homeland Security snatched him from his home in New York and took him to an immigration detention centre; he was then transferred to another facility in Louisian
entries.content:
Mahmoud Khalil was completing a master’s degree at Columbia University when, in March 2025, plain-clothed officers from the Department of Homeland Security snatched him from his home in New York and took him to an immigration detention centre; he was then transferred to another facility in Louisiana, more than 1,000 miles away. As a green card holder, Khalil has permanent US residency, but secretary of state Marco Rubio had determined that his continued presence in the country would have “adverse foreign policy consequences for the United States”, and sought his deportation under a legal provision dating back to the McCarthy era. Khalil was released on bail in June 2024 after a federal judge ruled his detention unconstitutional, but the Trump administration is still trying to have him removed.

Khalil – who was born to Palestinian parents in a refugee camp in Syria – had been targeted because of his advocacy on behalf of pro-Palestinian protesters during campus protests over Columbia University’s links to Israel. They were calling for Columbia to cut its ties with Israeli academic institutions and companies profiting from Israel’s onslaught on Gaza; in response, the university called in the NYPD. There was no suggestion that Khalil had done anything unlawful, and no criminal charges were brought against him; the government had simply identified him as an influential pro-Palestinian voice on campus, and for that reason alone they wanted him gone. He spent a total of 104 days in detention, missing the birth of his son.

Khalil recounts this Kafkaesque ordeal with a quiet fury in his memoir, No Land to Stand On. The episode is a damning snapshot of the Trump administration’s creeping authoritarianism and the cruelty of its immigration enforcement policy. Khalil was a high-profile detainee whose case drew considerable public scrutiny; he had access to lawyers, and was eventually able to extricate himself. Many of his fellow prisoners at the facility, hailing from places as diverse as Georgia, Romania, Senegal, Nepal, El Salvador and Chechnya, were less fortunate. They languish in detention for months on end, at the mercy of an opaque and glacially slow legal bureaucracy, “forgotten in a system designed to forget them”.

Khalil notes that the private ownership of the detention centre produced a perverse incentive structure. It “was not operated by the government, it was operated by shareholders. By people who made money when beds were filled and lost money when they were empty … Every man in this facility was a line item on a balance sheet. Every day we spent here was revenue.” This might explain why, whenever an asylum claim is successful, the state appeals the decision as a matter of course, needlessly extending the applicant’s detention by many more months. So much for the land of liberty.

At Columbia, too, the prerogatives of the private sector impinge on the public interest. The university, Khalil quips, “turned out to be a real estate empire with a campus attached”; its board of trustees is “not so much a neutral administrative body as a deeply ideological one … drawn overwhelmingly from finance, real estate, corporate law, and weapons manufacturers”. So when students called out the university’s entanglement with a state credibly accused of committing war crimes, the college administration treated it “as a crisis to be managed rather than a grievance to be heard”.

In the meantime, a broad coalition characterised by reading groups, fundraising bake-sales and solidarity with anti-Zionist Jewish groups was smeared as an antisemitic hate movement. There was much hand-wringing about student safety, at least some of which was in bad faith: “When pro-Israel students showed up at our events to film and harass us, the administration called it a legitimate expression of campus discourse. When we held a silent vigil, they described it as a security risk.” People may quibble over who is harassing whom in any given flashpoint, but one thing is undeniable: only those on one side of this argument are at risk of being spirited away by unidentified agents of the state on spurious pretexts.

Khalil dislikes being referred to as an activist because the term implies some degree of volition, when in reality he had no choice: “From the moment I was born Palestinian, my existence was political.” His personal backstory, told here in parallel with the account of his arrest and detention, is indeed shaped by political turmoil. As a teenager he was shot in the leg by Bashar al-Assad’s security forces; in 2013, aged 18, he fled Syria for Lebanon, where eventually he ended up working for the British embassy in Beirut. It was there that he met his future wife, a US citizen, before moving to New York in 2022.

What happened next is a warped travesty of the American dream: having grown up under a brutal dictatorship, Khalil settles in the US and exercises its much-vaunted political liberties, only to be locked up without charge alnd threatened with deportation. Palestinians, he concludes, “are the exception to every rule the supposed free world claims to hold sacred”. Given the horrors of the past three years, it’s hard to disagree.

entries.title: ‘The damage was much worse than I had imagined’: the shocking inside story of Salman Rushdie’s survival
entries.summary: After ​the writer was stabbed in a horrific attack, his wife started making a video diary of his recovery. The clips are featured in a new film from Alex Gibney, who drew on Dennis Potter to create a powerful portrait of Rushdie’s tumultuous lifeEliza Griffiths was at home in New York, drinking a second cup of coffee one August morning in 2022, when her phone rang. She answered it to a frantic fri
entries.content:
Eliza Griffiths was at home in New York, drinking a second cup of coffee one August morning in 2022, when her phone rang. She answered it to a frantic friend, who told her the man she had married just a year earlier, and who had set off the previous night for a speaking engagement nearly 400 miles away, had been hurt. “What kind of hurt?” she panicked. Turning on the television, she was assaulted by blurry images of chaos on stage as audience members surged to the rescue. Her husband, Sir Salman Rushdie, had been stabbed multiple times and was fighting for his life.

Within days of desperately chartering a plane to fly her to Rushdie’s hospital bedside, not knowing if he was alive or dead, Griffiths – a poet and photographer who works under her full name Rachel Eliza Griffiths – had begun to make a video diary recording his treatment and recovery. “When it had become likely that I was going to survive,” says Rushdie drily, “I said to Eliza we need to make a record of this. By which I meant something very modest: maybe she would take a picture of me on her iPhone every couple of days just to document the recovery, but Eliza had bigger ideas.”

One of her first ideas was that it needed to be shot not on a phone but with a proper camera. “I explicitly remember when the box arrived with my camera,” Griffiths says. “I cried because it was reconnecting me to my identity as an artist. The person I used to be, even just 24 hours ago, was being returned to me. It was giving both of us this permission to continue to be artists and tell our stories together.”

The couple are sitting in separate rooms of their New York home to tell their shared story over video link. Griffiths is warm and animated, as the memories rush out. Rushdie is more reserved and sardonic, smartly turned out, with only a black lens over his right eye to attest to the horrific injuries he suffered.

Both have already published memoirs about the experience: Rushdie’s Knife, in 2024 and Griffiths’ The Flower Bearers earlier this year. Now they are the subjects of an unflinching film, Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie, which combines Griffiths’ video diary with archive footage from the period following the fateful day in 1989 when a fatwa was issued against Rushdie for the offence allegedly caused to Islam by the supposed blasphemy of his fourth novel, The Satanic Verses. Iran’s then supreme leader, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini called for the execution of the 41-year-old author and his publishers, forcing him into hiding, where he remained, under armed guard, for nine years.

It is hard to say which time zone of the film is more viscerally shocking: the grisly footage of Rushdie being stitched and stapled back together in 2022, or the murderous hatred that roars out from news headlines in the months and years following the fatwa. In the US, the office of the Riverdale Press newspaper is firebombed after it runs an editorial about the book defending free expression; in Pakistan, six people are killed in riots; in Japan, a translator is stabbed to death; in Italy, another translator is stabbed in his home, while, in London, an effigy of a mutilated Rushdie is paraded through the streets by a furious crowd, some of whom declare on camera that nothing less than hanging will satisfy them.

Incorporating the archive footage was the idea of Alex Gibney, an Oscar-winning documentary maker (his newest film is a four-hour study of Elon Musk) who was invited by Rushdie and Griffiths to direct – or, as he describes it, “curate” – the film. Rushdie was initially opposed to dredging up the past, reasoning that his attacker – known simply as “A” in both his memoir and the film – was “just one crazy kid”. “I don’t see it as being representative of a larger matter,” he insists. “I think I was unfortunate in that this person was motivated by who knows what influences, and at this venue where he came to attack me, there was absolutely no security protection at all.”

The venue he was speaking at was at the heart of an idealistic community at Chautauqua in upstate New York, whose naivety in not having a single security guard in the hall Rushdie now sharply questions. Yet just three years before the attack, at a talk hosted by the Guardian at the Sheldonian in Oxford for his Booker-shortlisted novel Quichotte, he was tetchy to find plainclothes police at the entrances, complaining that only in the UK was such security still deemed necessary. “Well the thing is,” he says now, “in the preceding 20 years, I’d done hundreds of public events all over the world with no trouble, and it didn’t seem necessary to surround the Sheldonian with armed men.”

As the film reveals, not everyone shared his confidence. The Palestinian-American historian Edward Said predicted that the main threat Rushdie faced would not be soon from a religious fanatic, but at some time in the future from a random individual. The film’s power lies in the connection it forges between the two time frames: it demonstrates that the body in the bed in 2022, with a destroyed eye bulging from its socket, is what happens if the right to free speech is violently and publicly opposed.

Griffiths, who is Rushdie’s fifth wife, was an 11-year-old growing up in Delaware when the fatwa was issued. Gibney was “a wayward film-maker in search of a career” who had made a few TV documentaries and was trying to write some scripts. “I was doing a lot of reading because I didn’t get much work, so I was well aware of Salman as a novelist and an essayist,” he says. “But I think we [he and his editor] had forgotten, too, how vast it was. You know, you go through a process, starting by saying, OK, let’s see what kind of clips there are about the fatwa, and we were stunned.”

He concedes that Rushdie would have preferred less of the footage. “Salman doesn’t want to be defined by this. He bristles, and I understand it. You want to be defined by your artistic work, not by the political opportunism of a down-on-his-luck tyrant. But at the same time, I think it was hugely important for the audience to understand just how global it was.”

Gibney’s original idea was to model the film on Dennis Potter’s hit 1980s TV series The Singing Detective, based on Potter’s experience of struggling with the chronic skin disease psoriasis. “The simple story is that he comes in, in terrible shape, and over the course of the series, he recovers physically. But in the meantime, his life passes before his eyes. He thinks about his childhood. He hallucinates … and he imagines bits and pieces of his life through his own detective fiction. Salman was on his own path with Knife, and in some ways, they kind of coalesced. But ultimately, I did the smart thing with a writer of Salman’s stature, which is just to use enormous portions of Knife as the narration for the film.”

Though Rushdie wryly complains that he is the only one of the trio to receive no production credits, apart from “based on the book by …” (Griffiths has two, as cinematographer and executive producer), it gives full range to his “free-associating” mind, flitting from literary citation to animation and movie excerpts.

In one scene, he recalls a famous image from Georges Méliès’ classic short of 1902, Le Voyage dans La Lune, of a spacecraft crashing into the eye of the moon. “This is the literary device known as foreshadowing,” he wrote in the memoir. The night before the attack, happy because he was in love and had just signed off the proofs for his next novel (2023’s Victory City), he sent Griffiths a photograph of the moon seen from his hotel balcony. “Here’s a man in the dark, ignorant of the danger that’s already very close … the future rushes at him while he sleeps … Except strangely it’s really the past returning, my own past rushing at me … a masked man with a knife seeking to carry out a death order from three decades ago.”

Seeing the image reproduced for reference in a printed text is nothing like experiencing it on the big screen, juxtaposed with Griffiths’ unstinting footage of what Rushdie described as “my bulging boiled-egg eye [hanging] out of my face, the iris improbably perched on the swollen white …”

Why did Griffiths – and by extension the film – put so much emphasis on the horror of Rushdie’s damaged eye? “I think for me, the camera is part of how unbearable it was, and the shock for anyone to see their loved one being so wounded, so damaged, so violently attacked by another human being,” she replies. “And so I feel that, though the camera could be a sort of screen, also it was so open and you can’t look away.”

She continues: “It’s a very intimate point of view from love between two people in a new marriage, and this is where we’re at. It was just I’m moved to pick up the camera, or I can’t believe we’re in this situation. The camera is real, and I’m not. This can’t be happening to us. But then I’m like: ‘Well, it’s real because I can see it in the camera.’”

In the early days, when Griffiths was filming by day and camping out in Rushdie’s hospital room by night, she knew she could not show him what he looked like, any more than she could reveal her own fear and distress, which spill out in a tearful selfie monologue. It was only after he was finally allowed home that she asked if he’d like to see it. “I hadn’t really sat by myself and looked at much of it either,” she says. “When we finally did look at it, we did it together, and then it kind of became: ‘Oh, this is bigger than us, and maybe other people need to see it.’”

For Rushdie, the viewing was a rollercoaster. “First of all, I thought I looked really much worse than I thought I looked – the damage was much worse than I had imagined it to be. And then I felt quite pleased because I thought I don’t look like that any more. I look like this. So it actually dramatised the recovery.”

The final minutes of the film show the couple revisiting the scene of the attack, and laying to rest some of the misrememberings. Early on, Rushdie berates himself for submitting to his attacker. “I ask myself: why didn’t I do anything? Why did I just stand there? Well, in the film, you see that I didn’t just stand there. I tried to get away from him. So memory and reality are sometimes at odds with each other, and the film becomes a third perspective.”

Gibney tried, and failed, to get an interview in jail with “A”, the destroyer, who was wrestled to the floor and whose motives remain a mystery. “I wanted to understand this story as a kind of healing film, which I think we all of us need, and also about their investment in their love for each other,” he says. “So while it’s gruesome in parts and difficult and deals with the dark places of the human psyche, nevertheless, it finds a way out to a really good place.”

Rushdie and Griffiths had been together for five years when the attack happened, having met at the opening night of a festival that he had co-founded and chaired for the writers’ charity PEN. Though they didn’t hide their relationship, they did not flaunt it either, so that at the time of the attack, few people beyond their immediate friends and family knew they were married. “Being private is part of my personality,” says Griffiths. While the attack shoved Rushdie back into the spotlight, it forced her into it for the first time. She recalls looking out on this new reality as the plane carrying her to her husband’s bedside landed on an airstrip packed with law enforcement troops and realising she was just going to have to deal with it, “which is another part of my personality”. In an epigraph to his memoir, Rushdie quoted Samuel Beckett: “We are other, no longer what we were before the calamity of yesterday.” How much do they feel they have been changed by what’s happened? “Well,” he says, “I’m better than maybe I have any business to be. And Eliza, too.”

He still travels back and forth to see his sons and grandchildren in the UK, and the couple will be with them for the film’s London premiere. Has the attack ever tempted them to leave Trump’s US, where the forces against free speech and human rights seem ever more entrenched and dangerous? “What, for Farage’s Britain?” scoffs Rushdie. I take it that’s a no, then.

entries.title: Children’s and teens roundup – the best new picture books and novels
entries.summary: A tiger’s tale; the young Henry VIII; a fantasy follow‑up from Katherine Rundell; small-town secrets; ghosts galore and moreOnce Upon a Tiger by Sarah Massini, S&S, £14.99Tiger is irate to find three cheeky human cubs climbing on his back – but when they refuse to be scared off, he becomes increasingly attached to them. A sweet, classic-feeling picture book fable, heightened by tender, expressive
entries.content:
Once Upon a Tiger by Sarah Massini, S&S, £14.99

Tiger is irate to find three cheeky human cubs climbing on his back – but when they refuse to be scared off, he becomes increasingly attached to them. A sweet, classic-feeling picture book fable, heightened by tender, expressive illustrations.

Mama’s Wedding by Circle Yuen, Lantana, £12.99

Mama is getting married, but Ruby has mixed emotions – how will Daddy Albert feel on the day? A gorgeous, nuanced picture book about blended families and new milestones.

I Am a Squirrel by Scott Rothman, illustrated by Tom Tinn-Dinsbury, Happy Yak, £7.99

Big brother won’t believe that little brother’s a squirrel, even though he loves gathering nuts and leaping from tree to tree. But wait – is it time for a hawk to join the game? A funny, acutely observed picture book about sibling dynamics and imaginary play.

The Mole Construction Company by Shingo Nagasaki, translated by Lisa Wilcut, Do Re Mi, £12.99

Oh no, the Squirrels’ treehouse is tipping over! Enter the Moles with cranes and diggers to rebuild in this hugely engaging 4+ read-aloud story, translated from Japanese and perfect for vehicle-loving preschoolers.

Three Brides for the Devil by Sally Nicholls, illustrated by John Broadley, Andersen, £12.99

Charismatic and wealthy, the Devil rides into town in search of an obedient wife. Will one of the widow’s three daughters fit the bill? This elegant, subversive revisiting of Bluebeard, fascinatingly illustrated in intricate pen and ink, will grip 7+ readers as well as older children.

Ghost and Toast by Phil Corbett, Piccadilly, £8.99

Trying to remember how he arrived in a haunted mansion, Ghost is surprised to find a cheery companion in Toast, a perfectly ordinary sentient slice of browned bread. Surreal jokes abound as the unlikely duo attempt to thwart the nefarious Croissant in this daft, delicious 7+ graphic novel.

Henry Tudor: The Incredible Diaries of Me! by Danny Wallace, illustrated by Tor Freeman, Simon & Schuster, £7.99

Eight-year-old Henry Tudor is the best at everything - especially making rude and obnoxious demands. When he’s challenged by a mysterious opponent, however, he’s forced to acknowledge that he might not be completely infallible in this highly illustrated, laugh-a-minute, subversively “historical” 7+ diary.

How the Rivermaid Grew Her Tail and Other West African and Caribbean Myths by Jessica Wilson, illustrated by Sophie Bass, words & pictures, £12.99

Weaving together the storytelling traditions of West Africa and the Caribbean, this lush, joyful 8+ collection offers tales ranging from the trickster Anansi to the Jamaican rivermaid of the title, describing the origins of each story with enticing details of food, culture and landscape. Wilson’s ornate text is enhanced by Bass’s boldly coloured, swirling illustrations.

The Haunting of Old Splinter by Jack Mackay, Rock the Boat, £8.99

When he makes a grisly discovery in his uncle’s sinister mansion, Peter wonders if the old stories are true. Can Old Splinter’s mysterious Wishing Claw actually grant wishes - and if so, at what cost? A superlatively creepy revisiting of The Monkey’s Paw for 8+, from a brilliant new horror writer.

Tackling Racism Together by AM Dassu, illustrated by Mia Saine, words & pictures, £10.99

Informative and timely, this straightforward little book, produced in partnership with Show Racism the Red Card, provides a broad understanding of racism and its impacts, looking at systemic inequality, how our views are formed and how we can challenge racism in all its forms. A classroom must for 8+ readers.

Impossible Creatures: The Neverfear by Katherine Rundell, Bloomsbury, £16.99

When a dear friend is kidnapped from the Glimt Midsummer Feast, Christopher and Anya must undertake a desperate series of tasks to win her release. Funny, bloody, and richly underpinned with classical mythology, Rundell’s return to the world of Glimourie is layered with powerful themes of conservation, love, sacrifice and hope for readers of 9+.

And Then We Screamed by Holly Bourne, Usborne, £9.99

In the small town of Maple Lakes, everything is perfect – until cheerleader Abigail starts screaming in the middle of an exam. As more girls follow suit, student journalists Clover and Brody investigate the cause, only to discover the sad, terrible secrets beneath the town’s tranquil exterior. A fiercely feminist, gripping and emotionally resonant thriller from a much-loved YA author.

Dead Girls by Beck Kubrick, Simon & Schuster, £12.99

When five teenage girls are found murdered in Clossdale, suspicion falls on 17-year-old Ash, daughter of notorious serial killer “Evil Evelyn”. Determined to clear herself, Ash devises a plan to stop the killings, teaming up with her foster sister and best friend. But the girls aren’t expecting to discover a dark conspiracy dating back through generations of power. This blackly comic, splendidly camp graphic novel is a must for YA slasher-film fans.

Then We’ll Be Happy by Alan Carrigan, Chicken House, £8.99

Seventeen-year-old Sam, who has cerebral palsy, just wants some control over his life. When an inaccessible bus bars him from a school trip, he decides to campaign for change – but soon finds himself well out of his comfort zone, confronting his own internalised ableism as he investigates what happiness might look like for him now, rather than in a remote future. Carrigan’s YA debut is a humorous, sometimes painful, deeply engaging account of coming of age as a disabled teenager.

Between Ghosts and Gods by Ann Sei Lin, Walker, £16.99

As a mortal, Kasu sold her soul to a demon; now she works in a lower-world gambling den, exchanging ghosts’ treasures for gambling tiles, and living virtuously in the hope of reincarnation. When Arun, a mortal prince, arrives in the underworld looking for his mother, Kasu wants nothing to do with him - but as she and Arun are drawn closer, she may risk all her hopes to help his quest. A lush, delectable dark YA fantasy, rooted in Chinese mythology.

entries.title: ‘We demand the truth’: Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee lead calls for proof of life of disappeared Eritrean writers
entries.summary: More than 180 writers sign letter renewing calls for information on 12 authors detained incommunicado since 2001 crackdown on free speech by Isaias AfwerkiMore than 180 writers have signed a letter to Eritrean president Isaias Afwerki calling for proof of life for 12 writers arrested in 2001.Nobel laureates Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee join prominent writers including Colm Tóibín, Elif Shafak, Is
entries.content:
More than 180 writers have signed a letter to Eritrean president Isaias Afwerki calling for proof of life for 12 writers arrested in 2001.

Nobel laureates Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee join prominent writers including Colm Tóibín, Elif Shafak, Isabel Allende, Ben Okri, Yann Martel, Kamila Shamsie and Tsitsi Dangarembga in signing the letter organised by PEN International and dated 18 September, marking 25 years since a government crackdown on the independent press. “Within days, Eritrea’s free press and the nation’s independent voices were systematically crushed,” opens the letter.

It lists 12 writers who have been held incommunicado since 2001, including the poet Amanuel Asrat and playwright and journalist Dawit Isaak.

“The families of these writers, the Eritrean people and the global literary community have been met with a painful and unlawful silence,” continues the statement. “To withhold all information regarding their health, location, and survival is a violation of international law and an act of cruelty.”

Along with Asrat and Isaak, the other writers named in the letter are Dawit Habtemichael, Fessehaye “Joshua” Yohannes, Mattewos Habteab, Medhanie Haile, Sahle “Wedi-ltay” Tsegazeab, Said Abdelkadir, Said Idris “Abu Are”, Seyoum Tsehaye, Temesgen Ghebreyesus and Yousif Mohammed Ali. Six of the writers were profiled in the Guardian in 2015.

The letter, signed by 188 writers in total, calls for “immediate, verified proof of life for all arbitrarily detained Eritrean writers and critics”.

Other signatories include Andrei Kurkov, Anthony Doerr, Chloe Aridjis, Lauren Groff, Lemn Sissay, Maaza Mengiste, Madeleine Thien, Margaret Busby, Max Porter, Philippe Sands, Preti Taneja, Tice Cin and Viv Groskop.

“Mr President, Eritrea’s future must be built with its brightest minds, not based on their suppression,” the letter adds. “No writer or journalist should be disappeared for peacefully expressing their views.”

Eritrea operates as a repressive dictatorship under Afwerki, with no national elections held since independence in 1993.

“We remain in solidarity with our missing colleagues, and we will not cease our efforts until they are free,” the letter concludes.

Earlier this year, PEN International launched a petition, open to the public, which also calls for proof of life.

“Twenty-five years is an unbearable length of time for any family to live without knowing whether a loved one is alive,”, said Burhan Sönmez, president of PEN International. “These writers have not disappeared from our memory. We will continue to speak their names, and we will continue to demand the truth about what happened to them.”

entries.title: Robert Macfarlane and Jackie Morris’ guide to 49 threatened British birds wins Wainwright book of the year
entries.summary: The Book of Birds is a twist on classic field guides from the creators of bestseller The Lost WordsThe Book of Birds by Robert Macfarlane and Jackie Morris, an illustrated guide to Britain’s threatened bird species, has been named as the Wainwright prize book of the year.Meanwhile, the prize’s children’s book of the year award went to Otherlands: An Illustrated Journey Through Earth’s Lost Worlds
entries.content:
The Book of Birds by Robert Macfarlane and Jackie Morris, an illustrated guide to Britain’s threatened bird species, has been named as the Wainwright prize book of the year.

Meanwhile, the prize’s children’s book of the year award went to Otherlands: An Illustrated Journey Through Earth’s Lost Worlds by Thomas Halliday, illustrated by Gavin Scott.

The Book of Birds features 49 species of declining or endangered birds, with text by Macfarlane alongside artwork by Morris. It’s a “twist on the classic field guides that inspired both authors, evoking the spirit and poetry of birds from avocet to yellowhammer”, wrote Patrick Barkham in a Guardian interview with the author-illustrator pair in May.

“There are three billion fewer birds in North America than 50 years ago; 600 million fewer in Europe,” said Macfarlane at the time. “Our skies are thinner, our springs quieter. This is a savage loss. We wanted, in paint and word, to pull birds back into focus and splendour – and warn against their vanishing.”

Macfarlane and Morris previously collaborated on the bestselling title The Lost Words, which was a response to a group of nature-related words, including acorn and wren, being removed from the Oxford Junior Dictionary because children were using them infrequently. The book was shortlisted for the 2018 prize. The following year, Macfarlane won the prize with his book Underland.

Along with its two overall winners, the Wainwright prize, which celebrates the best nature and conservation writing published in the UK, announced four further category winners: Ancient: Reviving the Woods That Made Britain by Luke Barley (nature writing), The Savage Landscape by Cal Flyn (conservation writing), The Danger of Small Things by Caryl Lewis (children’s fiction) and The Great Bear by Annie Booker (picture books). Macfarlane and Morris had topped the illustrative books category, while Halliday and Scott won in the children’s nonfiction category, before both books went on to be named overall winners.

Each of the category winners receive £500 each, while the overall winners receive an additional £2,500 each.

“As environmental and social challenges grow ever more urgent, it’s inspiring to see writers using their voices to deepen our connection with the natural world,” said prize director Alastair Giles.

The prize was founded in 2013 by Frances Lincoln and the Alfred Wainwright estate. Previous winners include James Rebanks, Merlin Sheldrake and Chloe Dalton, who took home last year’s book of the year award for Raising Hare, about rescuing a leveret during the pandemic.

entries.title: My Year in Paris With Gertrude Stein by Deborah Levy audiobook review – gripping vision of a fearless writer
entries.summary: A fictional British author in Paris sets out to explore Stein through the lens of her own friendships, in this inventive, perfectly paced portraitIt is late 2024, and an unnamed British author living in Paris is trying to write an essay on Gertrude Stein, the modernist writer and art collector. The author has been distracted by her friend Eva’s cat, who is lost and whose name is “it” in lower case
entries.content:
It is late 2024, and an unnamed British author living in Paris is trying to write an essay on Gertrude Stein, the modernist writer and art collector. The author has been distracted by her friend Eva’s cat, who is lost and whose name is “it” in lower case, which inevitably leads to confusion – has Eva lost her cat or her mind? (Her other friend, Fanny, has rechristened the cat Bob, to make talking about him easier.)

The Pennsylvania-born Stein was painted by Picasso, hung out with Hemingway and wrote strange, stream-of-consciousness prose long before James Joyce embarked on his masterwork Ulysses. Commercial success didn’t come until she was in her 60s with The Autobiography of Alice B Toklas, a biography of her partner and one of her more accessible books. Our narrator is an admirer of Stein’s work, yet she can be exasperated by it. “Sometimes, when I read her baffling and beguiling writing I want to smack it in the chops. [Stein] longed for her readers to find her, yet there was a part of her that could not bear to be found.”

A blend of fiction and biography, Deborah Levy’s ninth novel is read by voice actor Kristin Atherton; her narration is cool, precise and perfectly paced. We follow the author as she goes to Père Lachaise cemetery in search of Stein’s grave and where she reflects on the lives of other literary luminaries, and on her own friendships. The Stein who emerges in this unusual and gripping portrait is fearless, innovative and, the author notes, “so forward-looking that she never learned to reverse her Ford Model T”.

Available via Penguin, 3hr 54min

Further listening

Nonesuch

Francis Spufford, Faber, 15hr 29min

Set during the blitz, this genre-bending thriller finds Iris Hawkins, a smart young office clerk, navigating a chance encounter which propels her into a world of necromancy, time-travelling Nazis and a plot to assassinate Winston Churchill.

The Delusions

Jenni Fagan, Penguin, 8hr 19min

Fagan’s satirical novel about the afterlife centres on Edi, who works in “the largest soul terminus in existence” where she processes the newly dead and decides where they should go based on how they lived their lives. Read by the author.
